insertText.text: The advantages of the feel method are that it is quick and inexpensive, requires no laboratory equipment and it is useful for field assessments and preliminary soil classification. Its limitation is that results are subjective and depend on the experience of the person performing the test.

**Principle of diminishing returns:** When more and more units of a variable input (such as fertiliser or labour) are added to a fixed input (such as land), each extra unit eventually adds less to total output than the one before.

insertText.after: Principle of diminishing returns: When more
insertText.text: **Principle of substitution:** A farmer replaces one input or enterprise with another when it produces the same output at a lower cost (for example, machinery in place of hired labour).
**Principle of equi-marginal returns:** A limited resource earns the most when it is shared among enterprises so that the last unit used in each gives the same extra return.
**Principle of comparative advantage:** A farm or region gains by producing what it can produce at a lower opportunity cost than others, and trading for the rest.

**Principle of time value of money:** Money received today is worth more than the same amount received in the future, because it can be invested to earn interest; long-term investments are compared after discounting future returns.

insertText.text: **Maintenance ration:** The amount of feed an animal needs to keep its body weight and health constant without producing anything, covering basic body functions such as breathing, digestion and keeping warm.

insertText.after: Maintenance ration: The amount of feed
insertText.text: **Production ration:** The feed given in addition to the maintenance ration so that the animal can produce milk, eggs, meat, wool or work. It is rich in energy and protein.
**Growth ration:** The feed given to young animals for the growth of bones, muscles and organs. It is high in protein, minerals (calcium and phosphorus) and vitamins.
**Pregnancy (steaming-up) ration:** Extra feed given in the last two to three months of pregnancy for the growth of the foetus and to prepare the dam for giving birth and producing milk.

**Feed block technology.** Feed blocks (urea-molasses multinutrient blocks) are made by mixing molasses, urea, bran, minerals and a binder such as cement or lime, then pressing the mixture into solid blocks. Ruminants lick them slowly, so they supply nitrogen, energy and minerals that improve the digestion of poor-quality roughage during the dry season.

**Use of insect-based protein.** Insects such as black soldier fly larvae and termites are rich in protein and fat. The larvae can be reared cheaply on farm and kitchen waste, dried and ground into a meal that replaces part of the fishmeal or soya cake in poultry, pig and fish rations.
